title: adding iPerf3 dissector support
description:
iPerf3 is quite different from iPerf2 and so requires its own dissector.

Recognizes "control connection" messages (session cookies, connection request refusal, etc) and data (labeled with its length, UDP message have their sequence number parsed)

It registers with port 5201 which is unused by any other protocols on wireshark (including by the reserved service "targus-getdata1")

notes.body: changed the description
marked this merge request as **ready**
requested review from @JaapKeuter
I have some sample capture files I want to throw at this and see what it comes up with.
These are shared with you as well via other means.

First remark: Can you amend the commit message to adhere to the desired format. see [Writing a good commit message.](https://wiki.wireshark.org/Development/SubmittingPatches#writing-a-good-commit-message)
Looks good now.

Remark regarding TCP transport. The vary nature of TCP is that it is a streaming protocol. That means there are no given PDU boundaries. The PDU boundaries need to be present in the PDU themselves. Unfortunately the iperf creators were no protocol designers, so reused the same PDU's on TCP connections, like they do on UDP 'connections'. Contrary to TCP, UDP is a datagram protocol that does have PDU boundaries.
Would it be possible to hand off the Payload to the data dissector?
Would it be possible to add the interpretation of the State not only to the Info column, but also in the packet details?
Would it be possible to hand off the JSON part to the JSON dissector?
Would it be possible to add a configuration option to support 64 bit sequence numbers?
Would it be possible to add an expert item to an iperf3 UDP data packet whose sequence number does not match the previous iperf3 UDP data packet number + 1, thereby signalling packet loss?
The dissector has trouble keeping track of status when dealing with TCP bidir traffic. One of the final JSON PDUs is not picked up.

From what I see is that a `DISPLAY_RESULTS` code is at the end of the TCP PDU. So we need to keep track of the reported length to determine what part of the following TCP PDU is actually JSON, and what's the following State ID.

This can be done later.
Even though you think you are safe due to previous checks, please use value_string and val_to_str() instead.

@JaapKeuter I'm convinced it's impossible to usefully decode iPerf3 over TCP using the current desgmentation functionality.

There's not enough context to differentially decode 1) the server-to-client stream that's only payload (the test data sent with the reverse flag) from 2) a stream that starts with a cookie and then payload (the client-to-server test data) vs 3) the client-to-server control stream starting with a cookie followed by other control stuff vs. 4) the server-to-client stream starting with the PARAM_EXCHANGE message and then control stuff. And of course the control stream could abruptly end at any point with a 1 byte error code.

The control stream does set TCP_NODELAY though... so maybe if we assume that messages below ~40 bytes wont be fragmented then small individual packets will map to PDUs. Only the JSON messages would need to be desegmented. This would leave most of the code substantially the same. Thoughts on this as an approach? If not then it seems like the dissector should just not support TCP at all.

Also: we can track certain things per conversation - like only interpret a message as a cookie if it's the first frame of a conversation, set a "NOT_CONTROL_CONNECTION" flag if we ever detect a message that can't be interpreted as state/pre-json/cookie/json or if we see more than 7 or 8 1-byte messages. That would make it more robust for iperf tests with the -l flag set to 1,4, and 37. Thoughts on this also?
@dmendes-rh Good points. I'm trying to find some more time to dig into it more.
Hmm, with the latest commit I'm starting to miss the JSON results being recognized when looking at a simple UDP test. I just don't have the time for the next three weeks to look deeper into this.
You'll have to protect against the conversation not being found. If this returns NULL, dissector exceptions will be thrown.

conversation_get_proto_data is invoked once for UDP dissection and once for TCP dissection. In both cases, it is explicitly checked if NULL, and if it is, then the metadata for that conversation is initialized. Seems all good then, right?
Assuming we can rely on the TCP and UDP dissector already setting up conversations, we should be good.

The older code is confusing. The idea is that either 1) the 64 bit sequence number configuration preference being enabled by the user OR 2) reading "0" from the top 4 bits should tell you to use 64 bit sequence numbers.

If either of those are true then you need to read 8 bytes instead to get the sequence number. If not then you can use the 4 bytes you read in.

Some detailed review so far.

Have you fuzz tested this code? See tools/fuzz-test.sh for this. Try it with all kinds of iperf3 capture files and see what bugs fall out.

I've tried with all sort of bidirectional and parallel UDP and TCP traffic, having multiple iperf3 processes sending traffic on top of each other at the same time, with ~100k UDP packets out of order, with extremely low MTUs, with and without 64 bit sequence numbers, with -l set to be extremely high and low (including 1,4,37 for tcp). Maybe half are on localhost and half are actually over the network. It always seems to produce the output I expect.

Fuzztesting on that same set of ~25 captures for 30 iterations doesn't turn up any errors. When I do something unsafe it tends to break quickly when fuzztesting so I have to assume its mostly good.

The only current issue is that for some error conditions the server/client will write the error code to the client/server and this 4 byte message gets interpreted as the JSON length. And these error codes are plausible lengths ( up to 300) so theres no way to distinguish them.

commits_data.title: iperf3: improved TCP control data handling
commits_data.message:
iperf3: improved TCP control data handling

Cookie detection can only occur with the first packet of a TCP
conversation. Segmented JSON can now be reassembled. Will no
longer try and interpret packets as control messages if they
occur within a conversation which probably can't be the control
connection. This all assumes that TCP_NODELAY is set for the
control connection and that messages less than 38 bytes are not
segmented.

commits_data.title: iperf3: addition of new dissector for iPerf3
commits_data.message:
iperf3: addition of new dissector for iPerf3

Recognizes "control connection" messages (session cookies,
connection request refusals) and "test data" fields where
applicable (UDP sequence numbers are used to detect out-of-order
and lost packets). Currently naively assumes a 1-to-1
relationship b/w TCP segments and PDU boundaries.
